7.text: A young widow with small children becomes part of the heritage left by

8.text: a man. With the herd she passes to the heir of the deceased, and becomes his

9.text: wife. Otherwise she must go to her own family, leaving everything behind.

10.text: She may take the children to her own family, but then they forfeit every

11.text: right to the inheritance. An elderly widow with youthful sons retains the herd

12.text: after her husband’s death, and may hold possession of the property.¹

13.text: Among the Maritime Chukchee, until recent times, there was but little

14.text: property to be inherited. After the death of the father, the sons divide his

15.text: arms, nets, and seal-skins. The older son has a better share than the others;

16.text: for instance, the best rifle. The house also is frequently divided into parts,

17.text: because every son, when married, wants to have a house of his own. As

18.text: soon as he finds enough timber, he proceeds to construct a separate house.

19.text: With the Reindeer Chukchee, to divide the house into parts is a great wrong.

20.text: They would rather desert the house entirely. The Maritime Chukchee simply

21.text: break down the house, take away the skins, poles, etc., divide them among

22.text: themselves, and use them for their own purposes.
